lesson.menu_desc: Answering the regulator: regulator, oversight, scrutiny, disclosure, sanction, whistleblower, filing, safeguard, code of conduct, audit trail -- and the passive of obligation: be required to, be permitted to, be prohibited from -- 27 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 23 -- Regulatory Language -- Answering the Regulator
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 23 -- Regulatory Language
lesson.grammar_point: passive of regulatory obligation (be required to / be permitted to / be prohibited from + -ing)

listenings.text: Simone, it is Daniel from group compliance. A letter came in from the regulator this morning and I need you on the response, so here is the picture before we speak. We are under scrutiny on two points. The first is a filing. We are required to send the quarterly report within thirty days of the end of the period, and the last one went out on day thirty-four. That is late, it is our fault, and I do not want anybody in the room arguing about it. The second point is heavier. Someone inside the company used the whistleblower channel in March, and the regulator wants to know what we did about it. Two things to keep in your head while you draft. We are permitted to ask for an extension, but only once, and only in writing before the deadline. And we are prohibited from contacting the person who raised the concern, so nobody goes near that. What will save us is the audit trail. Every step of the internal review is logged, with a name and a date, and that is what oversight actually wants to see. Read the code of conduct before you write anything, because the language of the answer has to match the language of our own rules. If we get this right, the worst outcome is a warning. If we get it wrong, the sanction is a fine.

It is Thursday and I have the regulator's letter open in front of me for the third time. Two points, and they are not the same size. The late filing is a fact. We are required to send that report within thirty days, we sent it on day thirty-four, and the only clean answer is to say so in one sentence and then explain the safeguard we have put in place so it cannot happen again. Arguing about four days in front of oversight is how a small problem becomes a large one. The second point is the one that keeps me awake. Somebody used the whistleblower channel in March, and the regulator wants the story of what happened next. Here my language has to be exact. We are permitted to ask for an extension, but only in writing and only before the deadline, so if I want it I have to decide by Monday. We are prohibited from contacting the person who raised the concern, which means nobody in the business unit hears a name from me. And every line I write has to be provable from the audit trail, because a disclosure that cannot be evidenced is worse than no disclosure at all. I am reading the code of conduct tonight, and tomorrow I write the draft in the same words it uses.

extra_audio.text: First, the letter from the regulator arrives and you read it twice, marking exactly what the company is being asked to explain. Then, you check the code of conduct and the internal rules, because the answer has to use the same language the company uses about itself. After that, you pull the audit trail together, with a name and a date against every step of the internal review. Next, you decide whether you are required to answer inside the deadline or whether you are permitted to ask for an extension in writing. Finally, you send the filing, you keep the disclosure complete, and you never contact the person who raised the concern.
